name: Asshur
title: Son of Shem and ancestor of the Assyrians
summary: Asshur was one of Shem's five sons and a grandson of Noah. He is regarded as the patriarch of the Assyrians, and his name is used in the Bible to refer both to the person, the people, and the land of Assyria. In Genesis he is mentioned in the table of nations after the flood, where the origins of the peoples are described. Who built the Assyrian cities Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen is disputed, since Gen 10:11 can be interpreted to mean that either Nimrod or Asshur went out and founded them. Asshur's descendants, the Assyrians, played a central role in biblical history as one of Israel's most powerful adversaries.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy
keyEvents.description: Asshur is listed as one of Shem's five sons in the post-flood genealogy that describes the origins of the nations.

keyEvents.title: The Assyrian cities are built
keyEvents.description: According to Gen 10:11-12, the cities of Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen were built. The Hebrew text is ambiguous and can be understood either as Nimrod going into the land of Asshur and building these cities, or as Asshur himself going out and building them.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Asshur is also mentioned in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, where the sons of Shem are listed to show Israel's historical connection with other nations.

keyEvents.title: Balaam's Prophecy about Asshur
keyEvents.description: Balaam prophesies about Asshur's future in his final speech, predicting that ships from Kittim will afflict Asshur and Eber.

versions.summary: Asshur was one of Shem's sons and a grandson of Noah. He is regarded as the patriarch of the Assyrians and the founder of the Assyrian Empire. In Genesis, he is mentioned in connection with the table of nations after the flood, and his descendants played a central role in biblical history as one of Israel's most powerful enemies.
versions.title: Shem's Son and Patriarch of Assyria
versions.reason: [major] Gen 10:11 is ambiguous: some translations read 'From that land he [Nimrod] went out to Asshur' while others read 'From that land Asshur went out'. This presents an interpretive challenge. The description states that 'from the land of Asshur Nimrod went out', but the Hebrew text can be read either way. The description should be nuanced to reflect this ambiguity.; [major] Gen 11:10-11 concerns Shem's son Arpachshad and Shem's age, not a repetition of Asshur as Shem's son. Asshur is not explicitly mentioned in these verses. This reference is incorrect and should be removed or corrected.; [minor] Asshur can also be described as the 'founding father' or 'eponym' for the Assyrians, in addition to being called a 'patriarch'. His role should be expanded to better reflect his biblical function.; [minor] The phrasing 'founder of the Assyrian empire' is somewhat imprecise. The Bible mentions Asshur as the ancestor of the Assyrians, but it is Nimrod who in Gen 10:11 is linked to the building of Assyrian cities. This should be nuanced.; [minor] There are no footnotes regarding important historical, linguistic, and archaeological details related to Asshur as the eponym for Assyria, and the ambiguous reading of Gen 10:11.

footnotes.text: The name 'Asshur' (Hebrew אַשּׁוּר, Aššur) functions both as a personal name and as a geographical/ethnic designation for Assyria and the Assyrians. In biblical tradition, the name is used interchangeably to refer to the person, the land, and the people.

Gen 10:11 is one of the most debated verses in the table of nations. The Hebrew text can be read either as Nimrod going out to Asshur (the land) and building Nineveh, or as Asshur (the person) going out from there and building Nineveh. Different translations and commentators are divided on this issue.

The city of Asshur (modern Qal'at Sherqat in Iraq) was the first capital of the Assyrian Empire and an important religious center. Archaeological excavations led by Walter Andrae (1903–1914) uncovered temples and palaces dating back to the third millennium BCE.

In Mesopotamian religion, Asshur (Aššur) was also the name of the Assyrians' national god, who was closely linked to the city and the empire. The biblical tradition, however, links the name to a person in Shem's lineage.

According to rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 20b), Gen 10:11 is interpreted such that Asshur left the plain of Shinar because he did not want to participate in building the Tower of Babel, and as a reward was allowed to build four cities.
